vectors.name: normalize/basic/merges-structurally-identical-records
vectors.comment: A and B are structurally identical (target-blind signature, then refined to a fixpoint); the lexicographically smallest name (A) is kept as the representative and every reference to B is rewritten to A.

vectors.name: normalize/basic/empty-schema-returned-unchanged
vectors.comment: prune leaves an unsatisfiable root's fields alone (see prune/basic/unsatisfiable-root-keeps-its-own-fields), so there is no 'fewest records' question to answer for a schema that accepts nothing -- normalize returns it unchanged after the is_empty check short-circuits.

vectors.name: normalize/basic/output-order-is-alphabetical-not-declaration-order
vectors.comment: Sec3.3's canonical serialization order, principle 2: normalize merges structurally-identical records into one representative, which destroys any single well-defined 'original position' for the survivor -- output MUST instead be alphabetical (records by name, ordinal comparison). M is declared first, before the merge; B survives the Y/B merge as the lexicographically smaller name. Output order is B, M -- alphabetical -- not M, B, which is what declaration-order-of-survivors would give (M was declared before either Y or B). This is the exact disambiguating case that settled the principle-2 design question live against the Python reference: a case where the two candidate rules (declaration order vs. alphabetical) actually disagree, unlike a schema that happens to already be alphabetical, which would pass under either rule and prove nothing.

vectors.name: normalize/refinement/ref-targets-in-different-blocks-block-the-merge
vectors.comment: Sec6.8's partition refinement MUST iterate to a fixpoint, and this is the only vector that requires it to. M1 and M2 are identical under the target-blind local signature -- one Ref field each, same label, same cardinality -- so a first-pass-only implementation merges them and rewrites Top.m2, silently collapsing two schemas that are not equivalent. Only a second refinement round separates them, once A and B are known to be in different blocks (they differ by scalar kind and never merge). Nothing merges here: all five records survive unchanged. Verified against the Python reference.

vectors.name: normalize/refinement/records-differing-only-by-scalar-kind-do-not-merge
vectors.comment: Sec6.8's prose flags this exact bug -- 'an implementation that reads is-scalar-or-not as a bare boolean will silently merge a string field with an integer field' -- and until now no vector tested it. The local signature MUST discriminate scalar kind, not merely value-versus-node. Direct case with no Ref indirection, so it isolates the signature bug from the refinement bug its sibling vector covers.

vectors.name: normalize/refinement/records-differing-only-by-nullable-do-not-merge
vectors.comment: The nullable half of the same discrimination requirement. Same scalar kind, differing only in nullability, which Sec3.3 S-7 makes part of the Scalar's identity -- so A and B accept different documents and MUST NOT merge. An implementation whose local signature records kind but drops the nullable flag passes the sibling vector above and fails here.
